node-1.label: Patient presented with cough, dyspnea, and chest pain

node-2.label: 42-year-old woman with metastases to the brain and bone and a history of multiple lines of treatment

node-3.label: Symptoms initially included cough and dyspnea, which were temporarily relieved but later returned along with chest pain

node-4.label: No detailed physical examination findings were provided in the case report

attrs.why: CT evidence of a lung lesion with alveolar septal changes and pleural effusion, follow-up CT showing enlargement with more nodules and effusion, and plasma cfDNA/pleural fluid NGS supporting metastatic involvement all point to metastatic pulmonary disease. The completed expert panel now includes the pathologist, radiologist, and laboratory physician, all of whom unanimously favor metastatic pulmonary disease as the leading explanation given the known brain/bone metastases and progressive cough, dyspnea and chest pain. Confidence is held at 0.82, tempered only by the absence of confirmatory pleural cytology/histopathology.

Malignancy-related hypercoagulability keeps pulmonary thromboembolism a theoretical concern, but no CTPA or D-dimer results are available to support it, and the progressive nodular lung lesion with pleural effusion plus NGS support for metastasis favor metastatic disease. All three expert analyses (pathologist, radiologist, laboratory physician) regard thromboembolism as much less likely or unexcluded. Confidence remains 0.08.

Multiple prior treatment lines could cause immunosuppression, but no infection markers are available and the progressive nodular lung lesion with pleural effusion together with NGS support for metastasis favor metastatic disease. The pathologist, radiologist, and laboratory physician all consider infection less likely. Confidence remains 0.05.

Prior treatment lines could theoretically cause drug-induced lung injury, but no specific drug exposure or supportive imaging pattern is provided, and the CT progression and NGS evidence favor metastatic pulmonary disease. None of the expert analyses (pathologist, radiologist, laboratory physician) favor drug-induced lung injury. Confidence remains 0.05.

node-12.label: Malignant pleural effusion secondary to metastatic disease

attrs.why: Known brain/bone metastases, CT evidence of pleural effusion, follow-up CT showing increased effusion, and pleural fluid NGS supporting metastatic involvement suggest malignant pleural effusion. The pathologist, radiologist, and laboratory physician all agree the effusion is likely malignant, but pleural cytology and histopathology remain unavailable for gold-standard confirmation, so confidence stays 0.7.
